sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: More than half of diabetes patients are Asians, and their tolerance to antidiabetic drugs may differ from that of non-Asians. Oral semaglutide has recently gained attention for its advantages in glycemic and body weight control. However, its effects across different ethnic groups remain unknown.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: All available databases of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on oral semaglutide in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus were included. These databases provided detailed patient information, including HbA1c levels, body weight, and adverse events (AEs and serious adverse events [SAEs]).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Ten randomized controlled trials involving 7817 patients were included: six conducted in European and American populations and four in East Asian populations. In both the Asian and non-Asian patients’ subgroups, oral semaglutide 3, 7, and 14 mg was more effective in reducing HbA1c than placebo, and between-subgroups analysis showed that semaglutide 3, 7, and 14 mg was more effective in reducing HbA1c in the Asian patients’ subgroup than in the non-Asian patients’ subgroup. There were no significant differences between subgroups in the number of patients achieving HbA1c < 5%. Non-Asian patients with type 2 diabetes showed significant weight reduction with 7 mg and 14 mg oral semaglutide, and Asian patients reduced body weight only with 14 mg oral semaglutide. Between-subgroups analysis showed that 7 mg oral semaglutide was more effective for weight reduction in non-Asian patients than in Asian patients. In the analysis of the efficacy of oral semaglutide at weeks 26 and 52 in Asian and non-Asian patients, in Asian patients, the hypoglycemic efficacy of oral semaglutide at 3-, 7-, and 14-mg doses at week 52 was significantly lower than that at week 26. In non-Asian patients, there was no significant difference in the reducing HbA1c efficacy of these doses of oral semaglutide at weeks 26 and 52. The weight-reduction efficacy of all doses of oral semaglutide did not change significantly with treatment duration in either Asian or non-Asian patients. Compared with sitagliptin, oral semaglutide was more effective in HbA1c reduction and weight reduction in both Asian and non-Asian patients. Subgroup analysis showed that compared with sitagliptin, Asian patients received oral semaglutide to achieve greater efficacy (HbA1c and weight reduction) than non-Asian patients. In the analysis of adverse events, oral semaglutide, as compared with placebo, was not associated with serious adverse events in either subgroup. The incidence of other (not including series) adverse events was significantly higher in non-Asian patients receiving 7 mg and 14 mg oral semaglutide.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Oral semaglutide demonstrates superior efficacy in reducing HbA1c levels and a rapid onset of action in Asian patients. However, its efficacy appears to diminish with prolonged treatment in this population. Medium (7 mg)-dose oral semaglutide was associated with greater weight reduction in non-Asian patients than in Asian patients, but this difference was eliminated with higher doses. Additionally, doses of 7 mg or more of oral semaglutide are associated with a higher incidence of side effects in non-Asian patients.
Keywords: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, Oral semaglutide, Asian and non-Asian, Drug therapy, Meta, Analysis, Systematic review
Received 2024 Oct 24; Accepted 2024 Dec 16; Issue date 2025 Mar.

tr.td: In daily diabetes care, patients of different races respond differently to oral semaglutide. Also, there has been no previous meta-analysis of the efficacy of oral semaglutide in Asians.
We designed this meta-analysis and systematic review to uncover differences in the efficacy of oral semaglutide between Asians and non-Asians.

bold.italic: What was learned from the study?

tr.td: Oral semaglutide demonstrates superior efficacy in reducing blood HbA1c and rapid onset of action in Asian patients, although it shows decreased efficacy following prolonged treatment in Asian patients. Medium (7 mg)-dose oral semaglutide was associated with greater weight reduction in non-Asian patients than in Asian patients, but this difference was eliminated with higher doses. Additionally, doses of 7 mg or more of oral semaglutide are associated with a higher incidence of side effects in non-Asian patients.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: More than 10.5% of the world’s adult population has diabetes today, according to an epidemiological study conducted in 2021. China, India, and Pakistan have the highest prevalence of diabetes among people aged 20–79. This trend is expected to continue until 2045 [1]. It is therefore urgently necessary to find a treatment that maintains long-term blood HbA1c control while minimizing complications.

Activation of the GLP-1 receptor by native GLP-1 or GLP-1RAs promotes insulin secretion and reduces excessive glucagon secretion in a glucose-dependent manner, enhancing glycemic control [2]. In particular, the drug did not induce weight gain in patients, in part because semaglutide works through the autonomic nervous system to suppress appetite for fatty foods and delay gastric emptying after meals [3]. However, previous GLP-1RAs were all administered by subcutaneous injection, and some patients refused to use it for this reason.

Rybelsus (oral semaglutide) is a GLP-1 receptor agonist with 94% homology to GLP-1 in humans. As the first oral GLP-1RA, it combines semaglutide with salcaprozate sodium (SNAC), which overcomes the challenges of peptide absorption in the acidic conditions of the stomach [4]. Patients with type 2 diabetes have been demonstrated to have an improvement in HbA1c and weight with Rybelsus in randomized controlled trials (RCTs), including the PIONEER series. Rybelsus has also been evaluated as a safe treatment when compared with other diabetes medications.

Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disease because the different basic metabolic conditions between the races show different drug treatment results. Previous studies have found racial differences in the effects of antidiabetic agents such as SGLT-2i [5, 6]. There are only a few meta-analyses available on the efficacy and safety of oral semaglutide [7, 8], and there are no articles reporting the effects of oral semaglutide in different races. For that reason, we performed this meta-analysis to evaluate the differences in glycemic control and weight reduction with oral semaglutide in Asian and non-Asian patients with T2DM to summarize the possible trends in oral semaglutide dosage in different races.

sec.title: Data Sources and Searches
sec.p: PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov database, Cochrane Library, and CNKI databases were searched for randomized controlled trials comparing oral semaglutide with placebo or other active medicines in patients with type 2 diabetes. The main search terms were “Semaglutide”, “NN9535”, “T2DM”, and “type 2 diabetes mellitus”. This study has been registered at INPLASY (INPLASY202380046).

sec.title: Study Selection
sec.p: The document management software Endnote was used to import bibliographic information from each database search result. Two independent reviewers independently reviewed the titles and abstracts after deduplication. Full-text articles were reviewed when title and abstract were insufficient to verify eligibility.
Inclusion and exclusion criteria are shown in Fig. 1. The screening aimed to find studies assessing the efficacy and safety of oral semaglutide in both Asian and non-Asian patients.

caption.p: Literature search flow chart and screening criteria

sec.title: Quality Assessment and Data Extraction
sec.p: Cochrane Handbook v5.2 was recognized as the authority on quality assessment. The studies’ biases were assessed using this method [9]. Two researchers conducted the evaluation. After completing data extraction, the two Excel tables used in the study were compared to ensure consistency and accuracy. If there were any differences, they were resolved through negotiation. Characteristics collected included author name, publication year, NCT number, patient’s size and ethnicity, intervention, follow-up time point, etc. As for the results, due to the limited data published so far, the Asian and non-Asian study results were recorded separately. HbA1c changes and body weight changes were observed, as well as the occurrence of adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs). Priority extraction of data from published articles when no data is given in a published article and the data in ClinicalTrials.gov is used. As for the dosage of oral semaglutide, we extracted three doses (3, 7, and 14 mg), among which 7 mg and 14 mg are the doses that have been approved by the regulatory authorities.

sec.title: Data Synthesis and Analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed using Review Manager (RevMan) 5.4.1, a Cochrane’s bespoke software for writing Cochrane Reviews. Continuous and dichotomous variables were analyzed using weighted mean differences (WMD) and risk ratios (RR), respectively, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Fixed-effects models were used to compare groups, and a statistical test for heterogeneity (I2 > 50%) was used to measure heterogeneity. Sensitivity analyses and subgroup analyses were used to minimize heterogeneity; if unresolved, a random-effects model was applied. Subgroup analyses assessed the efficacy and safety differences of oral semaglutide between Asians and non-Asians. Sitagliptin and liraglutide were used as antidiabetic agents in the active arms.

sec.title: Study and Patient Characteristics
sec.p: A comprehensive search of the database initially identified 596 records. After 245 duplicate articles were excluded, 318 were further screened based on titles and abstracts, resulting in 301 records being excluded. Among the remaining 15 articles, one focused on obese patients instead of individuals with type 2 diabetes and four articles lacked documentation of key indicators such as blood HbA1c and body weight before and after treatment (as shown in Fig. 1).

A total of ten articles were incorporated into the meta-analysis, encompassing 7817 participants (2947 Asian patients and 4870 non-Asian patients), with study durations varying from 26 to 78 weeks [10–19]. Table 1 provides a detailed account of the patients’ characteristics at enrollment and baseline. Six trials were conducted in Europe and North America, two in Japan, and two in China. Notably, all studies received funding from Novo Nordisk. The ethnic distribution is shown in Fig. 2.

sec.title: Quality Assessment
sec.p: Cochrane Handbook v5.2 was utilized to assess the risk of bias in the included studies, with the bias assessment chart created in RevMan (Fig. 3). All studies were from the PIONEER series, and randomization was performed through an interactive web-response system in all studies from the PIONEER series. PIONEER 2 and 10 were open-label studies, deemed high risk for performance bias, while the others employed a double-blind design. All the studies adhered to established protocols and reported all prespecified outcome measures, both primary and secondary. Outcome data were collected using protocol-specified measures, and each study addressed the issue of missing outcome data, implementing appropriate measures to ensure that the absence of data did not significantly impact the estimated effect sizes of the interventions. Therefore, all studies were considered low risk of bias.

sec.title: Differences in Efficacy of HbA1c Reduction of Oral Semaglutide in Asian and Non-Asian patients
sec.p: To assess if oral semaglutide lowers blood HbA1c more effectively in Asian patients, data from PIONEER 9–12 trials (mainly in Japan and China) were compared with data from PIONEER 1–8 trials (mostly White Europeans and Americans). The impact of various doses on HAb1c reduction was then evaluated. Results indicated that three doses of oral semaglutide (3, 7, and 14 mg) significantly outperformed placebo in both Asian and non-Asian patients’ subgroups. The efficacy in the Asian patients’ subgroup was notably higher than in the non-Asian patients’ subgroup across all doses (Test for subgroup difference 3 mg: P = 0.0005; 7 mg: P = 0.0006; 14 mg: P = 0.002, Fig. 4).

caption.p: Effect of oral semaglutide on HAb1c compared with placebo in Asian or non-Asian patients

sec.p: We also assessed the number of patients achieving an HbA1c level of 5% post-treatment within these two subgroups. All doses demonstrated a therapeutic advantage in the Asian and non-Asian patients’ subgroup (Fig. 5). However, subgroup analyses showed no significant differences in HbA1c-lowering ability between the two groups (test for subgroup difference 3 mg: P = 0.2; 7 mg: P = 0.51; 14 mg: P = 0.86, Fig. 5).

caption.p: Effect of oral semaglutide on the number of people achieving glycemic control in Asian and non-Asian patients

sec.p: To further elucidate the treatment effects of oral semaglutide across different subgroups, we analyzed the percentage reduction in HbA1c at 26 weeks and 52 weeks. The HbA1c-lowering efficacy of all doses of oral semaglutide diminished over time [for Asian patients: WMD – 0.24, I2 = 0%, two studies (3 mg); WMD – 0.3, I2 = 0%, two studies (7 mg); WMD – 0.2, I2 = 0%, two studies (14 mg); non-Asian patients WMD – 0.03, I2 = 31%, two studies (3 mg); WMD – 0.1, I2 = 0%, two studies (7 mg); WMD – 0.05, I2 = 0%, four studies (14 mg)]. Subgroup analysis showed that long-term use of oral semaglutide was associated with reduced efficacy in Asian patients (3 mg: P = 0.003; 7 mg: P = 0.02; 14 mg: P = 0.05, Fig. 6). But not in non-Asian patients (3 mg: P = 0.13; 7 mg: P = 0.60; 14 mg: P = 0.25, Fig. 6). These results indicate that oral semaglutide works faster and is more effective in Asian patients initially, but this benefit diminishes after 52 weeks. Notably, this phenomenon was attenuated with increasing doses. Unfortunately, there are no data to determine the extent of this advantage at week 52.

caption.p: Short-term and long-term glucose-lowering ability of oral semaglutide in Asian and non-Asian patients

sec.p: The efficacy of different agents versus oral semaglutide was assessed in various subgroups. Except for the 3 mg dose (for Asian patients: WMD-0.1, p = 0.2; for Non-Asian: WMD 0.2, P < 0.002), other doses of oral semaglutide were more effective than sitagliptin in lowering blood HbA1c in both Asian (7 mg: WMD-0.6, P < 0.00001; 14 mg: WMD-0.9, P < 0.00001) and non-Asian patients’ subgroups (7 mg: WMD-0.3, P < 0.00001; 14 mg: WMD-0.5, P < 0.00001).

Although oral semaglutide demonstrated a therapeutic advantage over sitagliptin in both subgroups, this advantage was more pronounced in the Asian patients’ subgroup (test for subgroup difference: P = 0.003; P = 0.004; P < 0.0001). Both oral semaglutide and liraglutide are GLP-1 analogs with comparable pharmacological mechanisms [20]. The results indicated no significant difference in efficacy between 14 mg oral semaglutide and 0.9 mg liraglutide in Asian patients (WMD: – 0.2, P = 0.32). However, in the non-Asian population, a double dose of liraglutide (1.8 mg) did not exhibit similar efficacy to 14 mg oral semaglutide (WMD: – 0.3, P = 0.0005). This observation indicates that non-Asian patients exhibit greater therapeutic benefits from oral semaglutide compared to liraglutide. The results are shown in Fig. 7.

caption.p: Effect of oral semaglutide on HAb1c compared with other therapeutic drugs in Asian or non-Asian patients

sec.title: Differences in Efficacy of Weight Reduction of Oral Semaglutide in Asians and Non-Asians
sec.p: The same method was used to assess the effectiveness of 3-, 7-, and 14-mg doses of oral semaglutide for weight reduction in Asian and non-Asian subgroups. Non-Asians experienced more weight reduction with the 7-mg dose compared to Asian patients (for Asian patients: P = 0.24, for non-Asian patients: P = 0.0003, Fig. 8). However, when the dose was increased to 14 mg, patients in both subgroups lost significant weight (both of Asian and non-Asian patients, P < 0.00001).

caption.p: The efficacy of oral semaglutide in reducing weight values in Asian and non-Asian patients

sec.p: Due to significant body weight differences by race, percentage weight reduction was compared, showing in non-Asian patients, semaglutide at a dose of more than 7 mg resulted in weight reduction, but in Asian patients, only 14 mg resulted in weight reduction [for non-Asian patients 3 mg: WMD 0.44, P < 0.35 (two studies); 7 mg: WMD – 1.05, P < 0.28 (two studies); 14 mg: WMD – 2.6, P < 0.00001 (two studies); for non-Asian patients: 3 mg WMD – 0.81, P < 0.09 (two studies); 7 mg WMD – 2.05, P < 0.0004 (two studies); 14 mg WMD – 3.58, P < 0.00001 (four studies), Fig. 9]. This finding is consistent with the results of previous analyses, indicating high confidence in the results. This suggests that the minimum effective dose of oral semaglutide in non-Asian patients was lower than that in Asian patients.

caption.p: The efficacy of oral semaglutide in percent weight reduction in Asian and non-Asian patients

sec.p: The long-term effects of oral semaglutide were also assessed at 26 and 52 weeks. The results showed that the weight reduction effect of the drug was not attenuated at 52 weeks in either subgroup [for Asian patients 3 mg: WMD – 0.35, P = 0.29 (two studies); 7 mg: WMD – 0.26, P = 0.53 (two studies); 14 mg: WMD – 0.53, P = 0.29 (two studies). for non-Asian patients: 3 mg WMD – 0.02, P = 0.97 (two studies); 7 mg WMD 0.1, P = 0.73 (two studies); 14 mg WMD 0.23, P < 0.25 (four studies), Fig. [10]. This suggests that long-term use of semaglutide does not attenuate the weight-reduction effect of the drug. In the recent clinical trial of oral semaglutide for weight reduction (OASIS) [21], the dose was determined to be 50 mg, but data from trials evaluating whether long-term use of 50 mg of oral semaglutide results in weight regain are lacking.

caption.p: Short-term and long-term lose-weight ability of oral semaglutide in Asian and non-Asian patients

sec.p: When comparing the weight reduction effects of the DDP-4 inhibitor sitagliptin and liraglutide (Fig. 11), the results indicated that oral semaglutide demonstrated a weight reduction advantage in both subgroups. The results of subgroup analysis showed that compared with other drugs, the efficacy of oral semaglutide 7 mg and 14 mg was more obvious in Asian patients than in non-Asian patients. Results are presented in Fig. 11.

caption.p: Effect of oral semaglutide on weight reduction compared with other therapeutic agents in Asian or non-Asian patients

sec.title: Adverse Events
sec.p: As shown in Table 2, subgroup analyses were conducted based on the number of patients experiencing serious and other (not including series) adverse events during drug administration. The findings indicated that the proportion of patients with serious adverse events was statistically significant among both Asian and non-Asian patients. However, the occurrence of other (not including series) adverse events was significantly elevated with 7 mg (p = 0.04) and 14 mg (p < 0.00001) oral semaglutide in the non-Asian patients, whereas no significant increase was observed in the Asian patients (7 mg: p = 0.56, 14 mg: p = 0.42).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: An evaluation of the efficacy and safety of oral semaglutide in patients with type 2 diabetes from different ethnic backgrounds was conducted in this systematic review and meta-analysis. In order to determine whether oral semaglutide had a greater therapeutic effect on Asian than non-Asian patients, subgroup analyses were performed. To obtain relevant clinical trial data for different subgroups, we screened ten randomized controlled trials (RCTs) from the PIONEER series. Specifically, Pioneer 1–8 predominantly included non-Asian participants (European and North American patients), whereas PIONEER 9–12 primarily involved East Asian participants (Japan and China). The findings indicated notable disparities in the efficacy of oral semaglutide across various populations. It is plausible that the HbA1c-lowering effect of oral semaglutide was both more rapid and pronounced in the Asian patients compared to placebo, as this differential response persisted even with increasing doses of oral semaglutide. However, a subsequent assessment of the number of patients achieving a 5% HbA1c level after treatment showed no difference in treatment effect between the two subgroups. This is due to differences in HbA1c control baseline among different races.

The analysis of weight reduction indicated that the medium-dose (7 mg) oral semaglutide was more efficacious in non-Asian patients. However, it is important to consider that patterns of body weight and adipose tissue distribution vary significantly across different racial groups [22]. A subsequent meta-analysis that examined the percentage weight reduction associated with oral semaglutide showed that the lowest effective dose of oral semaglutide was lower in non-Asian patients than in Asian patients, but the difference in efficacy between subgroups was eliminated when the dose was increased. The pronounced HbA1c-lowering efficacy of GLP-1 agonist analogs in Asian patients has been attributed to several factors, primarily the observation that Asian patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) exhibit lower endogenous GLP-1 levels compared to their non-Asian counterparts [23]. This disparity may be associated with impaired GLP-1 secretion in Asian individuals with T2DM. In addition, this study compared the short-term and long-term efficacy of oral semaglutide for HbA1c control and weight reduction. Based on the current findings, the hypoglycemic efficacy of oral semaglutide in Asian patients may be elucidated by the previously proposed hypothesis. Specifically, the initially low endogenous GLP-1 levels in Asians were swiftly augmented by oral semaglutide following short-term administration. Consequently, oral semaglutide demonstrated a rapid onset of action and pronounced effectiveness in Asian individuals after a 26-week treatment period. However, by week 52, the advantage conferred by the loading dose had substantially diminished. This observation appears to elucidate the rapid attenuation of benefits associated with long-term oral semaglutide treatment in Asian patients. Correspondingly, the analyses that evaluated the percentage weight reduction with long-term oral semaglutide showed no reduction in efficacy with all doses of oral semaglutide, regardless of subgroup. The exact mechanism of GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight reduction is unclear, but they are thought to slow gastric emptying and possibly reduce appetite via central nervous system effects.

Recent research indicates that GLP-1 receptor agonists may curb the start of eating by inhibiting NPY/AgRP neurons in the arcuate nucleus and encourage the end of eating in the lateral para-brachial(PB) nucleus. [24]. In a study conducted this year, Zijun Chen from China employed advanced methodologies, including single-cell sequencing and optogenetics, to systematically investigate the lateral septal nucleus (LS) in mice. The study revealed a substantial presence of GLP-1 receptor-positive neurons within this brain region. Animal studies have demonstrated that GLP-1R-positive neurons play a crucial role in mediating appetite suppression and weight reduction induced by the GLP-1R agonist liraglutide [25]. Consequently, we infer that racial disparities in the efficacy of oral semaglutide for weight reduction (the minimum effective dose was lower in non-Asian patients) are more likely attributable to variations in the expression of neurons within the central nervous system, rather than differences in systemic GLP-1 metabolism. In addition to a placebo, we conducted a comparative analysis of oral semaglutide with sitagliptin and liraglutide, the latter being pharmacologically similar to oral semaglutide. Two significant findings emerged from this comparison. Firstly, the hypoglycemic effects and weight reduction associated with sitagliptin and liraglutide can be effectively substituted with oral semaglutide (Figs. 7 and 11). Secondly, in comparison to liraglutide, oral semaglutide (Fig. 7) demonstrates a superior efficacy in reducing blood HbA1c among non-Asian patients. Although both liraglutide and semaglutide are GLP-1 receptor agonist analogs, their modes and frequencies of administration differ. Oral semaglutide is administered once daily, whereas liraglutide is administered once weekly. This difference may suggest a more rapid attenuation of liraglutide in non-Asian patients; however, no studies have been conducted to analyze this phenomenon. Finally, the analysis of adverse events suggested that high-dose oral semaglutide was associated with a higher incidence of side effects in non-Asian patients, suggesting that physicians should pay close attention to gastrointestinal side effects during treatment in non-Asian T2DM patients.

Our study has limitations. First, all the studies of the non-Asian subgroup in this study were multicenter studies, and a small number of Asians were included in these studies. Although the baseline data of the studies within the subgroups were consistent, this still led to a slight bias in the results. However, it is undeniable that the study has highlighted the significance of race, even in the absence of other important variables. Second, since the Asian patients were all from Japan and China, the representation of Asian subjects was compromised, and subsequent studies should strive to include Central and South Asian patients. Third, due to the differences in drug dosage and administration time, fewer studies were included in each subgroup, and more studies are expected to be included in the future. Given these limitations, the results of this study should be interpreted with caution.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In summary, oral semaglutide shows superior efficacy in reducing HbA1c levels and a rapid onset of action in Asian patients, although its efficacy diminishes with prolonged treatment in this population. A medium dose (7 mg) of oral semaglutide was associated with greater weight reduction in non-Asian patients compared to Asian patients; however, this difference was no longer observed at higher doses. Additionally, doses of 7 mg or higher were linked to a higher incidence of side effects in non-Asian patients.
